content:
Apple must respond by Monday to a complaint filed by Epic Games with Brazil's antitrust regulator. Epic alleges that Apple is interpreting its obligations under a recent App Store antitrust agreement in Brazil in a restrictive manner. Details below.

Some background

Two months ago, Apple announced it would allow developers to distribute apps in Brazil via alternative app stores.

The change was part of a settlement Apple reached in Brazil, ending a years-long antitrust investigation triggered by a complaint from Latin American e-commerce giant MercadoLibre over Apple's App Store rules.

Under the new terms, developers in Brazil can distribute iOS apps via alternative app stores and offer payment methods outside of Apple's IAP system.

Apple also introduced a new commission structure, including a 5% "Core Technology Fee" on sales of digital goods and services for apps distributed outside the App Store. More information on that structure is available here.

Epic questions Apple's implementation

According to Brazilian newspaper O Globo (via MacMagazine) today, Epic recently filed a petition with Brazilian antitrust regulator CADE alleging that Apple has erected "structural, technical, and access barriers" that undermine the practical viability of alternative app distribution channels.

Epic pointed out that, although the new terms in Brazil apply only to iOS apps, the agreement Apple reached with CADE "explicitly covers iPadOS."

The company also reportedly took issue with so-called "scare screens" that discourage users from installing apps from outside the App Store, and criticised the current installation flow as requiring nine steps, compared to six for Apple's current implementation in Europe.

O Globo reports that Epic added that Apple's original European installation flow required 15 steps, but after being forced to reduce it to six, "the download abandonment rate dropped from 65% to 25%."

Finally, Epic told CADE that Apple's reporting requirements "go far beyond what is necessary to calculate fees," and said this allows Apple to "monitor competitors' business models."

O Globo says CADE has given Apple until Monday to respond. Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
